For a planet in a circular orbit the geometric probability that it will transit its star is  

 P(transit) ≈ (R★ + Rp)/a  ≃  R★ / a           (Rp ≪ R★)

Hence, for two systems with the same stellar radius R★, the relative transit probabilities are inversely proportional to their orbital semi-major axes a.

Kepler’s third law for a planet of negligible mass gives  

 P² = 4π² a³ / (G M★)   ⇒   a ∝ (M★)^{1/3} P^{2/3}

Therefore  

 P(transit) ∝ R★ / a ∝ R★ / [ (M★)^{1/3} P^{2/3} ]

Because both host stars have the same radius, the ratio of the transit probabilities for Planet_1 (index 1) and Planet_2 (index 2) is

 P₁/P₂ = ( M₂^{1/3} P₂^{2/3} ) / ( M₁^{1/3} P₁^{2/3} )

Given  
• P₁ = P₂ / 3    (Planet_1’s period is three times shorter)  
• M₁ = 2 M₂     (Planet_1’s host star is twice as massive)

Insert these:

 P₁/P₂ = ( M₂^{1/3} P₂^{2/3} ) /
          ( (2 M₂)^{1/3} (P₂/3)^{2/3} )
        = 1 / [ 2^{1/3} · 3^{-2/3} ]
        = 3^{2/3} / 2^{1/3}

Numeric value:  

 3^{2/3} ≈ 2.08 , 2^{1/3} ≈ 1.26  

 P₁/P₂ ≈ 2.08 / 1.26 ≈ 1.65

So Planet_1 is about 1.65 times more likely to transit than Planet_2. The observers should therefore target Planet_1.

Answer: D
